Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Baikalsk Administration: FAIL (-0.85, -0.9) — Issued and deleted travel warning.
- Federal Authorities: FAIL (-0.9, -0.85) — Scrubbed reports and downplayed risks.
Local administration in Baikalsk warned against travel to Shelekhov after a young lab worker died of pneumonia following suspected plague exposure, prompting rapid censorship.

The Poison:
Scrubbing public health warnings creates acute panic and hoarding of antibiotics rather than building trust through open communication.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing public relations damage control with public safety (WHO vs WHAT), officials sacrificed transparency to protect regime optics.

Social Physics Analysis:
Authorities ran a classic Smart Selfish maneuver. Instead of practicing transparent risk disclosure, they manufactured a vacuum of information by deleting warnings, projecting calm while panic spread.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Suppression of vital health data breeds systemic contagion risks.

The Unavoidable Truth: Censoring disease alerts accelerates public panic and distrust.

The Unavoidable Lie: Deleting social media posts erases the underlying contagion threat.

Alethekanon:
Bureaucratic survival instincts override epidemiological truth, substituting censorship for containment.

Awwthekanon:
When people are terrified of a hidden plague, silencing their questions only deepens their suffering. Transparency is the only true medicine for fear.

Brothekanon:
Classic government move: panic everyone with a travel ban, then pretend nothing happened by deleting the tweet. Smooth.

When leaders hide the truth to save face, they trade human safety for hollow illusions of control.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Officials in Russia’s Irkutsk region advised against traveling to a town where a hospital patient may have died of plague. They later deleted the post. — Meduza

The administration of Baikalsk, a city in the Irkutsk region, published a Telegram post urging residents not to travel to Shelekhov, a satellite town of Irkutsk where a hospital patient may have died of pneumonic plague. It deleted the post two hours later, People of Baikal reported.

Actual Article Body:
The administration of Baikalsk, a city in the Irkutsk region, published a Telegram post urging residents not to travel to Shelekhov, a satellite town of Irkutsk where a hospital patient may have died of pneumonic plague. It deleted the post two hours later, People of Baikal reported.

The outlet also said the national television channel Ren TV had deleted five posts about the plague’s spread in Shelekhov from its social media.

Before that, Alexei Tsydenov, the head of Buryatia, edited a post stating that the woman who died of plague had not traveled to the region. He revised the wording about the cause of death, writing that the woman had “possibly died of plague.”

On October 2, media reported that Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old patient at the Shelekhov District Hospital, died of pneumonic plague. Authorities have not yet confirmed this, saying only that it involves a suspected case of an “especially dangerous infection.” Residents of Shelekhov and Irkutsk are buying up antibiotics effective against the plague pathogen amid the rumors, People of Baikal reported.

Russia last registered a case of plague in 2016, when a 10-year-old child fell ill in the Altai Republic.
